title: Περίφαντι ἐοικώς
about: Ajax kills Hippothous, who was dragging Patroclus’ body by the foot, and then Phorcys; the Trojans give ground. The Argives would have won glory beyond Zeus’ share, but Apollo, in the shape of the herald Periphas, urges Aeneas on. Aeneas knows the god, shames Hector and the leaders into turning, and the fight goes on around the body: Aeneas and Lycomedes strike men down, and Ajax holds the Achaeans close about Patroclus. Mist covers the battle round the body while the rest of the army fights in sunlight, and two Achaeans, Thrasymedes and Antilochus, do not yet know that Patroclus is dead.

sentences.t:
ἤτοι τὸν Λήθοιο Πελασγοῦ φαίδιμος υἱὸς
Ἱππόθοος ποδὸς ἕλκε κατὰ κρατερὴν ὑσμίνην
δησάμενος τελαμῶνι παρὰ σφυρὸν ἀμφὶ τένοντας
Ἕκτορι καὶ Τρώεσσι χαριζόμενος·
sentences.l:
Him, indeed, of Lethus the Pelasgian the glorious son
Hippothous was dragging by the foot through the strong battle,
having bound a strap about the tendons by the ankle,
to Hector and the Trojans gratifying;
sentences.i: Hippothous, the glorious son of Lethus the Pelasgian, was dragging him by the foot through the strong battle, having bound a strap about the tendons by the ankle, to gratify Hector and the Trojans;
sentences.n: τὸν ‘him’ is the body of Patroclus, who is not named until 299. Λήθοιο Πελασγοῦ is ‘of Lethus the Pelasgian’ (epic genitive -οιο), and φαίδιμος υἱός ‘glorious son’ is Hippothous, the stock φαίδιμος in the table’s ‘glorious’. ἤτοι is printed as one word. ἕλκε is the imperfect without augment, ‘was dragging’, and ποδός is the genitive of the part taken hold of; δησάμενος is an aorist middle participle ‘having bound’, with τελαμῶνι ‘with a strap’ and σφυρόν ‘ankle’, τένοντας ‘tendons’. Hector is gratified (χαριζόμενος) by the dragging.

sentences.t:
τάχα δ’ αὐτῷ
ἦλθε κακόν, τό οἱ οὔ τις ἐρύκακεν ἱεμένων περ.
sentences.l:
and soon to him came evil, which for him
not anyone held back, though eager.
sentences.i: and soon evil came upon him, which none could hold back from him, however eager they were.
sentences.n: αὐτῷ ‘to him’ is Hippothous. τό is the relative ‘which’, pointing back to κακόν ‘evil’, and ἐρύκακεν is a reduplicated aorist of ἐρύκω ‘hold back, keep off’. ἱεμένων περ is a genitive plural participle of ἵεμαι ‘be eager’, ‘though they were eager’, that is, of those who wished to keep the evil off; they are not named.

sentences.t:
τὸν δ’ υἱὸς Τελαμῶνος ἐπαΐξας δι’ ὁμίλου
πλῆξ’ αὐτοσχεδίην κυνέης διὰ χαλκοπαρῄου·
sentences.l:
Him the son of Telamon, having rushed on through the throng,
struck at close quarters, through the bronze-cheeked helmet;
sentences.i: The son of Telamon rushed on through the throng and struck him at close quarters, through his bronze-cheeked helmet;
sentences.n: τὸν ‘him’ is Hippothous, and the son of Telamon is Ajax, who is named at 303 (Αἴαντος). ἐπαΐξας is an aorist participle of ἐπαΐσσω ‘rush at’. πλῆξ’ is πλῆξε, the aorist of πλήσσω ‘strike’. αὐτοσχεδίην is a feminine accusative used as an adverb, ‘at close quarters’, and χαλκοπαρῄου is the genitive of χαλκοπάρῃος, ‘bronze-cheeked’, of a helmet with bronze cheek-pieces.

sentences.t:
ἤρικε δ’ ἱπποδάσεια κόρυς περὶ δουρὸς ἀκωκῇ
πληγεῖσ’ ἔγχεΐ τε μεγάλῳ καὶ χειρὶ παχείῃ,
ἐγκέφαλος δὲ παρ’ αὐλὸν ἀνέδραμεν ἐξ ὠτειλῆς
αἱματόεις·
sentences.l:
And split the horse-haired helmet about the spear’s tip,
struck by the great spear and by the stout hand,
and the brain by the socket ran up from the wound,
bloody;
sentences.i: The helmet, thick with horsehair, split about the tip of the spear, struck by the great spear and the stout hand, and the brain ran up by the socket out of the wound, bloody;
sentences.n: ἤρικε is an aorist of ἐρείκω ‘tear, split’, used here without an object, ‘split, burst’. ἱπποδάσεια κόρυς is the helmet ‘thick with horsehair’; πληγεῖσ’ is an aorist passive participle, ‘struck’, with the datives ἔγχεΐ … χειρί ‘by the spear … by the hand’. ἀκωκῇ is the dative of ἀκωκή ‘tip’. αὐλός is a ‘tube’; whether the socket of the spear-head or the channel of the wound is meant is not known for certain, and ‘socket’ is the usual reading. ὠτειλῆς is the genitive of ὠτειλή ‘wound’, and αἱματόεις ‘bloody’ stands last in the clause for emphasis.

sentences.t:
τοῦ δ’ αὖθι λύθη μένος, ἐκ δ’ ἄρα χειρῶν
Πατρόκλοιο πόδα μεγαλήτορος ἧκε χαμᾶζε
κεῖσθαι·
sentences.i: His might was loosed on the spot, and from his hands he let the foot of great-spirited Patroclus fall to the ground, to lie there;
sentences.n: τοῦ ‘of him’ is Hippothous again, and λύθη μένος is ‘the might was loosed’, his strength failing as he dies. ἐκ … ἧκε is ἐξῆκε with the preverb apart from its verb (tmesis), from ἵημι ‘let go, let fall’; χαμᾶζε is ‘to the ground’ (-ζε is a form of -δε). μεγαλήτορος is the genitive of μεγαλήτωρ ‘great-spirited’, a stock epithet, here of Patroclus. κεῖσθαι ‘to lie’ is an infinitive of result.

sentences.t:
ὃ δ’ ἄγχ’ αὐτοῖο πέσε πρηνὴς ἐπὶ νεκρῷ
τῆλ’ ἀπὸ Λαρίσης ἐριβώλακος,
sentences.l:
and he close beside him fell face down upon the corpse,
far from rich-soiled Larisa,
sentences.i: and he fell on his face upon the corpse, close beside him, far from rich-soiled Larisa,
sentences.n: ὃ δ’ is Hippothous; αὐτοῖο is the epic genitive of αὐτός, ‘him’, the corpse, and ἄγχι ‘close’ takes it. πρηνής is ‘face down’. ἐριβώλακος, from ἐριβῶλαξ ‘rich-soiled’, is the stock epithet of a fertile place. Larisa is named as the place he is far from, so it is his home; the next unit speaks of the parents who reared him.

sentences.t:
οὐδὲ τοκεῦσι
θρέπτρα φίλοις ἀπέδωκε, μινυνθάδιος δέ οἱ αἰὼν
ἔπλεθ’ ὑπ’ Αἴαντος μεγαθύμου δουρὶ δαμέντι.
sentences.l:
and not to his parents
dear, the repayment for rearing did he give back, and short-lived for him his life
was, subdued by great-hearted Ajax with a spear.
sentences.i: and he did not repay his dear parents for his rearing, and his life was short-lived, since he was overcome by great-hearted Ajax with his spear.
sentences.n: τοκεῦσι is a dative plural, ‘parents’, with φίλοις ‘dear’. θρέπτρα is ‘the repayment for rearing’, what a son owes his parents for bringing him up, and ἀπέδωκε is an aorist ‘gave back’. μινυνθάδιος ‘short-lived’ goes with αἰών ‘life’; ἔπλεθ’ is ἔπλετο ‘was’. δαμέντι is an aorist passive participle in the dative, agreeing with οἱ ‘for him’, ‘subdued’, and ὑπ’ Αἴαντος is the agent, ‘by Ajax’.

sentences.t: Ἕκτωρ δ’ αὖτ’ Αἴαντος ἀκόντισε δουρὶ φαεινῷ·
sentences.l: And Hector in turn at Ajax cast with a shining spear;
sentences.i: Hector in turn cast at Ajax with his shining spear;
sentences.n: αὖτ’ is αὖτε ‘in turn’; the cast answers Ajax’s blow. ἀκόντισε takes the genitive Αἴαντος, ‘cast at’, and δουρὶ φαεινῷ is the stock ‘shining spear’.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ὃ μὲν ἄντα ἰδὼν ἠλεύατο χάλκεον ἔγχος
τυτθόν· ὃ δὲ Σχεδίον μεγαθύμου Ἰφίτου υἱὸν
Φωκήων ὄχ’ ἄριστον, ὃς ἐν κλειτῷ Πανοπῆϊ
οἰκία ναιετάασκε πολέσσ’ ἄνδρεσσιν ἀνάσσων,
sentences.l:
But he, looking straight at it, avoided the bronze spear
by a little; and he, Schedius, great-hearted Iphitus’ son,
of the Phocians by far the best, who in famous Panopeus
homes used to dwell, ruling over many men,
sentences.i: But Ajax, seeing it coming straight at him, avoided the bronze spear, though only just; and Hector—Schedius, the son of great-hearted Iphitus, by far the best of the Phocians, who lived in famous Panopeus, ruling over many men there—
sentences.n: ὃ μὲν is Ajax, who sees the cast coming (ἄντα ἰδών) and avoids it; ὃ δὲ is Hector, who has turned to another man. Σχεδίον is an accusative, the object of βάλ’ in 309, and the long description of Schedius runs on until τὸν resumes him there, so the English breaks off with a dash. Φωκήων is ‘of the Phocians’, and ὄχ’ ἄριστον ‘by far the best’. ναιετάασκε is an iterative imperfect of ναιετάω ‘dwell’ (‘used to dwell’), and οἰκία is ‘homes’. ἀνάσσων is ‘ruling’.

sentences.t: τὸν βάλ’ ὑπὸ κληῗδα μέσην·
sentences.l: Him he struck beneath the collar-bone, the middle part;
sentences.i: him he hit beneath the middle of the collar-bone;
sentences.n: τὸν ‘him’ picks up Schedius, and βάλ’ is βάλε, the aorist of βάλλω ‘strike’. κληῗδα is the accusative of κληΐς ‘collar-bone’ (the diaeresis is as printed), and μέσην ‘middle’ goes with it. The unit ends at the ano teleia in the middle of the line.

sentences.t:
διὰ δ’ ἀμπερὲς ἄκρη
αἰχμὴ χαλκείη παρὰ νείατον ὦμον ἀνέσχε·
sentences.l:
and through, right through, the topmost
bronze point beside the lowest shoulder stood out;
sentences.i: and the very tip of the bronze point passed straight through and stood out at the bottom of the shoulder;
sentences.n: διὰ … ἀμπερές is ‘through, right through’, with διά as an adverb. ἄκρη agrees with αἰχμή ‘point’ and means ‘topmost’, so the end of the point came out. νείατον is ‘lowest’, so the point comes out low on the shoulder; the line does not say more exactly where. ἀνέσχε is the aorist of ἀνέχω, ‘held up, stood out’.

sentences.t: δούπησεν δὲ πεσών, ἀράβησε δὲ τεύχε’ ἐπ’ αὐτῷ.
sentences.l: and he fell with a thud, and his armour clattered upon him.
sentences.i: and he fell with a thud, and his armour clattered upon him.
sentences.n: δούπησεν ‘thudded’ and ἀράβησε ‘clattered’ are aorists, and πεσών is the aorist participle ‘having fallen’. τεύχε’ is τεύχεα, ‘armour’.

sentences.t:
Αἴας δ’ αὖ Φόρκυνα δαΐφρονα Φαίνοπος υἱὸν
Ἱπποθόῳ περιβάντα μέσην κατὰ γαστέρα τύψε·
sentences.l:
And Ajax in turn Phorcys, the wise-minded son of Phaenops,
bestriding Hippothous, in the middle of the belly struck;
sentences.i: Ajax in turn struck Phorcys, the wise-hearted son of Phaenops, as he stood over Hippothous, in the middle of the belly;
sentences.n: Φόρκυνα is the accusative ‘Phorcys’, the object of τύψε (the aorist of τύπτω ‘strike’), and Φαίνοπος υἱόν is ‘son of Phaenops’. δαΐφρονα is the stock epithet: ‘wise’ and ‘fierce’ are both argued for, and the table’s ‘wise-minded’ (in the English ‘wise-hearted’) keeps the first. περιβάντα is an aorist participle of περιβαίνω with the dative Ἱπποθόῳ, ‘standing astride’ him, over the fallen man; μέσην … γαστέρα is ‘the middle of the belly’.

sentences.t:
ῥῆξε δὲ θώρηκος γύαλον, διὰ δ’ ἔντερα χαλκὸς
ἤφυσ’·
sentences.l:
and broke the hollow of the breastplate, and through, the bowels, the bronze
drew out;
sentences.i: and broke the hollow of his breastplate, and the bronze drew his bowels out through it;
sentences.n: ῥῆξε is the aorist of ῥήγνυμι ‘break’, with Ajax, or his spear, understood. γύαλον is ‘the hollow’, the curved plate of the breastplate, and θώρηκος is its genitive. διά is again an adverb, ‘through’, and ἤφυσ’ is ἤφυσε, from ἀφύσσω ‘draw out’.

sentences.t: ὃ δ’ ἐν κονίῃσι πεσὼν ἕλε γαῖαν ἀγοστῷ.
sentences.l: and he, in the dust having fallen, took the earth in the crook of his arm.
sentences.i: and he fell in the dust and clutched the earth in the crook of his arm.
sentences.n: ὃ δ’ is Phorcys. κονίῃσι is a dative plural in -ῃσι, ‘in the dust’, and ἕλε is the aorist of αἱρέω, ‘took, seized’. ἀγοστῷ is a dative of ἀγοστός, ‘the crook of the arm’; the exact sense of the word is not known, and this is the usual reading.

sentences.t: χώρησαν δ’ ὑπό τε πρόμαχοι καὶ φαίδιμος Ἕκτωρ·
sentences.l: And back gave way the front-fighters and glorious Hector;
sentences.i: Both the foremost fighters and glorious Hector gave way;
sentences.n: χώρησαν is the aorist of χωρέω ‘give way, withdraw’, and ὑπό belongs to it (tmesis, ‘back’). πρόμαχοι ‘front-fighters’ and φαίδιμος Ἕκτωρ ‘glorious Hector’ are the table’s renderings; τε … καί joins the two subjects.

sentences.t:
Ἀργεῖοι δὲ μέγα ἴαχον, ἐρύσαντο δὲ νεκροὺς
Φόρκυν θ’ Ἱππόθοόν τε, λύοντο δὲ τεύχε’ ἀπ’ ὤμων.
sentences.l:
and the Argives shouted loudly, and drew off the corpses,
Phorcys and Hippothous, and were loosing the armour from their shoulders.
sentences.i: and the Argives shouted aloud, dragged off the corpses, Phorcys and Hippothous, and began stripping the armour from their shoulders.
sentences.n: ἴαχον is ‘shouted’, an aorist of ἰάχω, and ἐρύσαντο is ‘drew off, dragged away’. Ἱππόθοόν is printed with both accents, as the edition has it; it is the accusative of Ἱππόθοος. λύοντο is a middle imperfect, ‘were loosing (for themselves)’, the stripping begun and not finished, and ἀπ’ ὤμων is ‘from the shoulders’.

sentences.t:
ἔνθά κεν αὖτε Τρῶες ἀρηϊφίλων ὑπ’ Ἀχαιῶν
Ἴλιον εἰσανέβησαν ἀναλκείῃσι δαμέντες,
Ἀργεῖοι δέ κε κῦδος ἕλον καὶ ὑπὲρ Διὸς αἶσαν
κάρτεϊ καὶ σθένεϊ σφετέρῳ·
sentences.l:
There, again, the Trojans, by the Ares-loved Achaeans
to Ilios would have gone up, overcome through want of might,
and the Argives would have won glory even beyond Zeus’ due measure
by strength and by power their own;
sentences.i: Then once more the Trojans, overcome by the Achaeans, dear to Ares, through their want of might, would have gone up into Ilios, and the Argives would have won glory beyond the share Zeus had allotted, by their own strength and power;
sentences.n: κεν with the aorist indicatives εἰσανέβησαν and ἕλον makes a past that did not happen: ‘would have gone up’, ‘would have won’. ἀναλκείῃσι is a dative plural, ‘through want of might’, with δαμέντες ‘overcome’. αἶσα is ‘due measure, share’ (the table has κατ’ αἶσαν ‘in due measure’), so ὑπὲρ Διὸς αἶσαν says that the Argives’ glory would have gone past what Zeus had decreed. κάρτεϊ and σθένεϊ are datives, ‘strength’ and ‘power’, as in the table, and σφετέρῳ ‘their own’ agrees with both.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ αὐτὸς Ἀπόλλων
Αἰνείαν ὄτρυνε δέμας Περίφαντι ἐοικὼς
κήρυκι Ἠπυτίδῃ, ὅς οἱ παρὰ πατρὶ γέροντι
κηρύσσων γήρασκε φίλα φρεσὶ μήδεα εἰδώς·
sentences.l:
but Apollo himself
urged on Aeneas, in form likened to Periphas,
the herald, Epytus’ son, who beside his old father
as herald was growing old, knowing kindly counsels in his mind;
sentences.i: but Apollo himself urged Aeneas on, taking the form of Periphas, the herald, son of Epytus, who grew old as a herald beside his aged father, a man who knew kindly counsels in his mind;
sentences.n: αὐτός ‘himself’ marks the god’s own part in turning the fight. ὄτρυνε is ‘urged on’ (aorist), and δέμας Περίφαντι ἐοικώς is ‘likened to Periphas in form’, δέμας being an accusative of respect. Ἠπυτίδῃ is a patronymic in the dative, ‘Epytus’ son’, agreeing with κήρυκι. οἱ is the weak pronoun ‘to him’ and most naturally points back to Aeneas, but the Greek does not name the aged father. γήρασκε is an imperfect of γηράσκω ‘grow old’, and κηρύσσων ‘as herald’. φίλα is here ‘kindly’; ‘his own’ is the other possible sense, and the stock phrase fits a loyal servant either way.

sentences.t: τῷ μιν ἐεισάμενος προσέφη Διὸς υἱὸς Ἀπόλλων·
sentences.l: Having made himself like to that man, addressed him Zeus’ son Apollo:
sentences.i: Making himself like that man, Apollo, the son of Zeus, said to him:
sentences.n: τῷ ‘that man’ is Periphas; ἐεισάμενος is an aorist middle participle meaning ‘having made himself like’, and μιν ‘him’ is Aeneas. προσέφη is ‘addressed’. The speech that follows is Apollo’s, in the guise of Periphas.

sentences.t:
Αἰνεία πῶς ἂν καὶ ὑπὲρ θεὸν εἰρύσσαισθε
Ἴλιον αἰπεινήν;
sentences.l:
“Aeneas, how could you, even beyond a god, protect
steep Ilios?
sentences.i: “Aeneas, how could you defend steep Ilios, even in defiance of a god?
sentences.n: The vocative Αἰνεία is singular, but the verb εἰρύσσαισθε is plural: Apollo speaks to Aeneas for all the Trojans. πῶς ἂν with the optative asks ‘how could you …?’, and εἰρύσσαισθε is an aorist optative middle of εἰρύομαι ‘protect, guard’. ὑπὲρ θεόν is ‘beyond a god’: the sense is ‘in spite of a god’s will’, as ὑπὲρ Διὸς αἶσαν at 321; Ἴλιον αἰπεινήν is the stock ‘steep Ilios’.

sentences.t:
ὡς δὴ ἴδον ἀνέρας ἄλλους
κάρτεΐ τε σθένεΐ τε πεποιθότας ἠνορέῃ τε
πλήθεΐ τε σφετέρῳ καὶ ὑπερδέα δῆμον ἔχοντας·
sentences.i: as I have indeed seen other men, trusting in their strength and power and manliness and their own numbers, and holding a people that was without fear;
sentences.n: ὡς δὴ ἴδον is ‘as I have indeed seen’, and the verb that goes with the other men, ‘defend their city’, is left to be understood from the question. ἴδον is the unaugmented aorist of ὁράω. πεποιθότας is a perfect participle ‘trusting’, taking the datives κάρτεΐ, σθένεΐ, ἠνορέῃ, πλήθεΐ (‘strength’, ‘power’, ‘manliness’, ‘multitude’), with σφετέρῳ ‘their own’. ὑπερδέα is a rare word read as ‘fearless’ (ὑπέρ + δέος, ‘beyond fear’); its exact sense is not certain, and δῆμον ἔχοντας is ‘having a people’.

sentences.t:
ἡμῖν δὲ Ζεὺς μὲν πολὺ βούλεται ἢ Δαναοῖσι
νίκην·
sentences.l:
but for us Zeus indeed far more wishes than for the Danaans
victory;
sentences.i: but Zeus wishes victory far more for us than for the Danaans;
sentences.n: ἡμῖν δέ ‘but for us’ is set against the Danaans in the next words. βούλεται is ‘wishes, prefers’, and πολύ is an adverb, ‘far more’, with ἢ Δαναοῖσι ‘than for the Danaans’; νίκην ‘victory’ is held back to the next line.

sentences.t: ἀλλ’ αὐτοὶ τρεῖτ’ ἄσπετον οὐδὲ μάχεσθε.
sentences.l: but you yourselves tremble boundlessly and do not fight.”
sentences.i: but you yourselves are in fear beyond all measure, and do not fight.”
sentences.n: αὐτοὶ ‘you yourselves’ turns on the Trojans: the god has already told them they have Zeus’ favour. τρεῖτ’ is τρεῖτε, the present of τρέω ‘tremble, flee in fear’. ἄσπετον is the neuter accusative of ἄσπετος ‘boundless’ used as an adverb, ‘beyond measure’, and οὐδὲ μάχεσθε is ‘and do not fight’. The speech ends here.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἔφατ’, Αἰνείας δ’ ἑκατηβόλον Ἀπόλλωνα
ἔγνω ἐς ἄντα ἰδών, μέγα δ’ Ἕκτορα εἶπε βοήσας·
sentences.l:
So he spoke, and Aeneas far-shooting Apollo
knew, looking straight at him, and loudly to Hector he said, having shouted:
sentences.i: So he spoke, and Aeneas, looking him straight in the face, knew Apollo who shoots from afar, and shouted loudly to Hector:
sentences.n: ὣς ἔφατ’ ‘so he spoke’ closes Apollo’s speech. ἑκατηβόλον is ‘far-shooting’ (in the English ‘who shoots from afar’), the stock epithet of Apollo. ἔγνω is the aorist of γιγνώσκω, ‘recognised’, and ἐς ἄντα ἰδών is ‘looking straight at (him)’, ‘face to face’. μέγα βοήσας is ‘having shouted loudly’, and Ἕκτορα with εἶπε is the person addressed, in the accusative.

sentences.t:
Ἕκτόρ τ’ ἠδ’ ἄλλοι Τρώων ἀγοὶ ἠδ’ ἐπικούρων
αἰδὼς μὲν νῦν ἥδε γ’ ἀρηϊφίλων ὑπ’ Ἀχαιῶν
Ἴλιον εἰσαναβῆναι ἀναλκείῃσι δαμέντας.
sentences.l:
“Hector, and you other leaders of the Trojans and of the allies,
shame, indeed, now, this is, by the Ares-loved Achaeans
to go up to Ilios, overcome through want of might.
sentences.i: “Hector, and you other leaders of the Trojans and of the allies, this is a shame indeed: to go up into Ilios, overcome through want of might by the Achaeans, dear to Ares.
sentences.n: Ἕκτόρ is a vocative, printed with its accent so. ἀγοί is ‘leaders’, and Τρώων … ἐπικούρων ‘of the Trojans and of the allies’ is as in the table. αἰδώς is ‘shame’, a shameful thing, and ἥδε γ’ is ‘this indeed’. εἰσαναβῆναι is an aorist infinitive of εἰσαναβαίνω ‘go up into’, and the unspoken subject is ‘us’, which δαμέντας ‘overcome’ (accusative plural) agrees with; ἀναλκείῃσι is ‘through want of might’, as at 320.
sentences.mark: Aeneas rouses Hector and the leaders

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἔτι γάρ τίς φησι θεῶν ἐμοὶ ἄγχι παραστὰς
Ζῆν’ ὕπατον μήστωρα μάχης ἐπιτάρροθον εἶναι·
sentences.l:
But still, for one of the gods says, standing near beside me,
that Zeus, highest counsellor of battle, is a helper;
sentences.i: But still, for one of the gods says, standing close by me, that Zeus, the highest master of battle, is a helper;
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ ἔτι γάρ is compressed: ‘but there is still (hope), for …’, with the hope left unsaid. φησι … εἶναι is ‘says that … is’, with the accusative Ζῆν’ (= Ζῆνα). ὕπατον is ‘highest’, μήστωρα μάχης is ‘counsellor, master of battle’ (the table’s μήστωρ, with its genitive), and ἐπιτάρροθον ‘helper’ is a rare word of obscure formation; all three agree with Ζῆν’. Whose helper is not said. παραστάς is an aorist participle ‘standing beside’.

sentences.t:
τώ ῥ’ ἰθὺς Δαναῶν ἴομεν, μηδ’ οἵ γε ἕκηλοι
Πάτροκλον νηυσὶν πελασαίατο τεθνηῶτα.
sentences.l:
therefore straight at the Danaans let us go, and let not them, at ease,
bring Patroclus near to the ships, dead.”
sentences.i: So let us go straight at the Danaans, and let them not bring Patroclus, dead, to the ships at their ease.”
sentences.n: τώ ῥ’ is τῷ ῥα, ‘therefore, then’. ἰθύς is ‘straight’, and ἴομεν is a subjunctive of εἶμι, ‘let us go’. μηδ’ … πελασαίατο is an aorist optative (3rd plural middle, -αίατο for -αιντο) in a wish, ‘let them not bring’, with οἵ γε ‘they’ the Danaans, and ἕκηλοι ‘at ease’ is the table’s word. νηυσίν is ‘to the ships’, and τεθνηῶτα is a perfect participle, ‘dead’. The speech ends here.

sentences.t: ὣς φάτο, καί ῥα πολὺ προμάχων ἐξάλμενος ἔστη·
sentences.l: So he spoke, and far in front of the front-fighters leaping out he stood;
sentences.i: So he spoke, and leaping out far in front of the foremost fighters, he took his stand;
sentences.n: ὣς φάτο is ‘so he spoke’ with no augment. ἐξάλμενος is the aorist participle of ἐξάλλομαι ‘leap out’, and πολύ is ‘far’, with the partitive genitive προμάχων ‘in front of the front-fighters’. ἔστη is the aorist ‘took his stand’.

sentences.t: οἳ δ’ ἐλελίχθησαν καὶ ἐναντίοι ἔσταν Ἀχαιῶν.
sentences.l: And they were whirled round and stood opposite the Achaeans;
sentences.i: They wheeled round and took their stand facing the Achaeans;
sentences.n: οἳ δ’ is the Trojans. ἐλελίχθησαν is an aorist passive of ἐλελίζω ‘whirl round’, the table’s ‘were whirled round’ and ‘wheeled round’; ἔσταν is the root aorist ἔστησαν, ‘stood’, and ἐναντίοι Ἀχαιῶν is ‘opposite the Achaeans’, with a genitive.

sentences.t:
ἔνθ’ αὖτ’ Αἰνείας Λειώκριτον οὔτασε δουρὶ
υἱὸν Ἀρίσβαντος Λυκομήδεος ἐσθλὸν ἑταῖρον.
sentences.l:
There in turn Aeneas Leiocritus wounded with a spear,
the son of Arisbas, Lycomedes’ good companion.
sentences.i: Then Aeneas in turn wounded Leiocritus, the son of Arisbas, with his spear, the good companion of Lycomedes.
sentences.n: ἔνθ’ αὖτ’ is ‘then, in turn’: Aeneas now does what Ajax and Hector did. οὔτασε is the aorist of οὐτάω ‘wound’; the line does not say yet whether Leiocritus is killed. Λειώκριτον and υἱόν are accusatives, and Ἀρίσβαντος is ‘of Arisbas’. Λυκομήδεος is a genitive in -εος (= -ους), and ἐσθλὸν ἑταῖρον is ‘a good companion’.

sentences.t:
τὸν δὲ πεσόντ’ ἐλέησεν ἀρηΐφιλος Λυκομήδης,
στῆ δὲ μάλ’ ἐγγὺς ἰών, καὶ ἀκόντισε δουρὶ φαεινῷ,
sentences.l:
And him, fallen, pitied Ares-loved Lycomedes,
and stood, coming very close, and cast with a shining spear,
sentences.i: Lycomedes, dear to Ares, pitied him as he fell, and took his stand very close and cast with his shining spear,
sentences.n: τὸν … πεσόντ’ is ‘him, having fallen’, and ἐλέησεν is the aorist of ἐλεέω ‘pity’. ἀρηΐφιλος is ‘dear to Ares’, the stock epithet of a warrior. στῆ is ἔστη without augment, ‘took his stand’, and ἰών ‘coming’ is the participle of εἶμι; ἀκόντισε is ‘cast’. The opening words of 352 repeat these with another man’s name.

sentences.t:
καὶ βάλεν Ἱππασίδην Ἀπισάονα ποιμένα λαῶν
ἧπαρ ὑπὸ πραπίδων, εἶθαρ δ’ ὑπὸ γούνατ’ ἔλυσεν,
sentences.l:
and struck Hippasus’-son Apisaon, shepherd of the people,
in the liver beneath the midriff, and at once he loosed his knees,
sentences.i: and hit Apisaon, son of Hippasus, shepherd of the people, in the liver under the midriff, and at once loosed his knees,
sentences.n: Ἱππασίδην is a patronymic, ‘Hippasus’ son’, in the accusative with Ἀπισάονα, and ποιμένα λαῶν is the stock ‘shepherd of the people’. ἧπαρ ὑπὸ πραπίδων is ‘the liver, beneath the midriff’, where the spear went in. εἶθαρ is ‘at once’, and ‘loosed his knees’ means that his legs gave way under him and he went down dead.

sentences.t:
ὅς ῥ’ ἐκ Παιονίης ἐριβώλακος εἰληλούθει,
καὶ δὲ μετ’ Ἀστεροπαῖον ἀριστεύεσκε μάχεσθαι.
sentences.l:
who from rich-soiled Paeonia had come,
and moreover next after Asteropaeus used to be the best at fighting.
sentences.i: He had come from rich-soiled Paeonia, and next after Asteropaeus he used to be the best at fighting.
sentences.n: ὅς ῥ’ is the relative, ‘who’, pointing back to Apisaon. Παιονίης ἐριβώλακος is ‘rich-soiled Paeonia’, and εἰληλούθει is the pluperfect of ἔρχομαι, ‘had come’. καὶ δέ is ‘and moreover’. μετ’ Ἀστεροπαῖον is μετά with the accusative, ‘next after Asteropaeus’, so Asteropaeus ranks first; ἀριστεύεσκε is an iterative imperfect of ἀριστεύω ‘be the best’ (‘used to be’), with the infinitive μάχεσθαι ‘at fighting’.

sentences.t:
τὸν δὲ πεσόντ’ ἐλέησεν ἀρήϊος Ἀστεροπαῖος,
ἴθυσεν δὲ καὶ ὃ πρόφρων Δαναοῖσι μάχεσθαι·
sentences.l:
And him, fallen, pitied warlike Asteropaeus,
and he too rushed, ready-minded, to fight the Danaans;
sentences.i: Warlike Asteropaeus pitied him as he fell, and he too rushed with a ready mind to fight the Danaans;
sentences.n: This line begins as 346 did: τὸν … πεσόντ’ ἐλέησεν, ‘pitied him as he fell’, now with ἀρήϊος ‘warlike’ Asteropaeus, who, like Lycomedes, then acts. ἴθυσεν is the aorist of ἰθύω ‘rush straight’. ὃ is the pronoun ‘he’, and καί ‘also’; πρόφρων is ‘with a ready mind’. Δαναοῖσι takes μάχεσθαι ‘to fight’, in the dative.

sentences.t: ἀλλ’ οὔ πως ἔτι εἶχε·
sentences.l: but in no way any longer could he;
sentences.i: but he could not do it any longer;
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ οὔ πως ἔτι εἶχε is ‘but in no way any more was he able’: εἶχε is the imperfect of ἔχω used with no object or infinitive, so what he could not do is left unsaid, and what stopped him is given in the next unit.

sentences.t:
σάκεσσι γὰρ ἔρχατο πάντῃ
ἑσταότες περὶ Πατρόκλῳ, πρὸ δὲ δούρατ’ ἔχοντο.
sentences.l:
for with shields they were shut about on every side,
standing around Patroclus, and in front the spears were held.
sentences.i: for they were shut about on every side with shields, standing around Patroclus, and spears were held out in front.
sentences.n: ἔρχατο is the pluperfect passive of εἴργω ‘shut in’, ‘were shut about’ (the table has ἔρχαται, ‘are shut about’), and the Achaeans standing round the body are the ‘they’ without being named. σάκεσσι is the dative plural of σάκος ‘shield’, and ἑσταότες is the perfect participle ‘standing’. ἔχοντο is the middle or passive of ἔχω, here ‘were held’; πρό is ‘in front’, and the exact shade of the middle is not certain.

sentences.t: Αἴας γὰρ μάλα πάντας ἐπῴχετο πολλὰ κελεύων·
sentences.l: for Ajax, greatly, went about to all of them, giving many orders;
sentences.i: for Ajax went round to every one of them, giving many orders;
sentences.n: ἐπῴχετο is the imperfect of ἐποίχομαι ‘go about to, go round’, and μάλα sharpens πάντας, ‘every one of them’. πολλὰ κελεύων is ‘ordering many things’, and what he ordered follows.

sentences.t:
οὔτέ τιν’ ἐξοπίσω νεκροῦ χάζεσθαι ἀνώγει
οὔτέ τινα προμάχεσθαι Ἀχαιῶν ἔξοχον ἄλλων,
ἀλλὰ μάλ’ ἀμφ’ αὐτῷ βεβάμεν, σχεδόθεν δὲ μάχεσθαι.
sentences.l:
neither any to give ground backwards from the corpse did he bid,
nor any to fight in front, outstanding above the other Achaeans,
but to stand very close about it, and to fight from near at hand.
sentences.i: He bade none give ground backwards from the corpse, nor any one of the Achaeans to fight out in front, conspicuous beyond the rest, but to stand very close about it and fight from near at hand.
sentences.n: οὔτέ … οὔτέ … ἀλλά is ‘neither … nor … but’, all depending on ἀνώγει ‘bade’ (imperfect). χάζεσθαι is ‘to give ground’, and ἐξοπίσω is ‘backwards’; προμάχεσθαι is ‘to fight as a front-fighter’, with ἔξοχον ἄλλων ‘outstanding above the others’ describing the man who would push ahead; Ἀχαιῶν is partitive with τινα (‘any of the Achaeans’), and the literal line joins it to ἄλλων. βεβάμεν is the perfect infinitive of βαίνω (= βεβάναι), ‘to stand firm’, with ἀμφ’ αὐτῷ ‘about it’, the corpse; σχεδόθεν is ‘from near at hand’.

sentences.t:
ὣς Αἴας ἐπέτελλε πελώριος, αἵματι δὲ χθὼν
δεύετο πορφυρέῳ, τοὶ δ’ ἀγχιστῖνοι ἔπιπτον
νεκροὶ ὁμοῦ Τρώων καὶ ὑπερμενέων ἐπικούρων
καὶ Δαναῶν·
sentences.l:
So Ajax enjoined, the huge one, and with blood the earth
was drenched, purple, and they, in close succession, fell,
dead, together, of Trojans and of allies of surpassing strength
and of Danaans;
sentences.i: So huge Ajax gave his instructions, and the earth was drenched with purple blood, and the dead fell one close upon another, all together, men of the Trojans and of their allies of surpassing strength and of the Danaans;
sentences.n: ὣς ‘so’ closes Ajax’s orders. ἐπέτελλε is the imperfect of ἐπιτέλλω ‘give instructions’, and πελώριος ‘huge’ is the stock word for Ajax’s size. δεύετο is from δεύω ‘wet, drench’ (not the δεύομαι ‘lack’ of the table), and πορφυρέῳ, ‘purple’, here describes dark blood. τοὶ δ’ is ‘and they’, the dead; ἀγχιστῖνοι is ‘in close succession’ in the literal line, as the table has it (the table’s English is ‘one close upon another’). Τρώων, ἐπικούρων and Δαναῶν are partitive genitives (‘some of …’), and ὑπερμενέων ‘of surpassing strength’ goes with ἐπικούρων.

sentences.t:
οὐδ’ οἳ γὰρ ἀναιμωτί γε μάχοντο,
παυρότεροι δὲ πολὺ φθίνυθον·
sentences.l:
for not even these without bloodshed were fighting,
but far fewer were perishing;
sentences.i: for the Danaans too did not fight without bloodshed, but far fewer of them were perishing;
sentences.n: οὐδ’ οἳ is ‘not even these’, the Danaans last named. ἀναιμωτί is ‘without bloodshed’, and μάχοντο is ‘were fighting’ with no augment. παυρότεροι is a comparative, ‘fewer’, strengthened by πολύ ‘by far’, and φθίνυθον is an imperfect of φθινύθω ‘waste away, perish’.

sentences.t:
μέμνηντο γὰρ αἰεὶ
ἀλλήλοις ἀν’ ὅμιλον ἀλεξέμεναι φόνον αἰπύν.
sentences.l:
for they were ever mindful
for one another through the throng to ward off steep slaughter.
sentences.i: for they were always mindful of warding off steep slaughter from one another throughout the throng.
sentences.n: μέμνηντο is a pluperfect of μιμνήσκομαι with the sense of an imperfect, ‘were mindful’, and it takes the infinitive ἀλεξέμεναι ‘to ward off’ (Homeric -έμεναι). ἀλλήλοις is ‘for one another’, and ἀν’ ὅμιλον is ‘through the throng’. φόνον αἰπύν is the table’s ‘steep slaughter’.

sentences.t:
ὣς οἳ μὲν μάρναντο δέμας πυρός, οὐδέ κε φαίης
οὔτέ ποτ’ ἠέλιον σῶν ἔμμεναι οὔτε σελήνην·
sentences.l:
So they, for their part, fought in the likeness of fire, and nor would you say
that either the sun was ever safe, or the moon;
sentences.i: So they fought like fire, and you would not say that the sun or the moon was safe;
sentences.n: οἳ μὲν is those round the body, answered by οἳ δ’ ἄλλοι at 370. δέμας πυρός is an accusative of respect, ‘in the likeness of fire’, as the table has it. φαίης is an optative with κε, ‘you would say’. σῶν is the accusative of σῶς ‘safe, whole’, ἔμμεναι is the infinitive ‘to be’, and the thought is that the mist hid the sun and the moon so thickly that one could not say they were still there, whole.

sentences.t:
ἠέρι γὰρ κατέχοντο μάχης ἐπί θ’ ὅσσον ἄριστοι
ἕστασαν ἀμφὶ Μενοιτιάδῃ κατατεθνηῶτι.
sentences.l:
for in mist they were held, over as much of the battle as the best
stood about Menoetius’ son, him who has died.
sentences.i: for they were enveloped in mist, over all that part of the battle where the best men stood about the dead son of Menoetius.
sentences.n: ἠέρι is the dative of ἠήρ ‘mist’, and κατέχοντο is a passive imperfect, ‘were held fast, enveloped’. ἐπί θ’ ὅσσον is compressed: the mist lay over just as much of the battle as the best men took up round the body. ἕστασαν is a pluperfect with the sense of an imperfect, ‘were standing’; Μενοιτιάδῃ is a patronymic, ‘Menoetius’ son’, that is Patroclus, and κατατεθνηῶτι is a perfect participle ‘him who has died’.

sentences.t:
οἳ δ’ ἄλλοι Τρῶες καὶ ἐϋκνήμιδες Ἀχαιοὶ
εὔκηλοι πολέμιζον ὑπ’ αἰθέρι, πέπτατο δ’ αὐγὴ
ἠελίου ὀξεῖα, νέφος δ’ οὐ φαίνετο πάσης
γαίης οὐδ’ ὀρέων·
sentences.l:
But the other Trojans and the well-greaved Achaeans
at ease were fighting under the aether, and spread was the ray
of the sun, sharp, and no cloud appeared over all
the earth nor the mountains;
sentences.i: But the other Trojans and the well-greaved Achaeans fought at their ease under the bright upper air, and the sharp ray of the sun was spread abroad, and no cloud was to be seen over all the earth or the mountains;
sentences.n: οἳ δ’ ἄλλοι answers οἳ μὲν at 366: the rest of the army, away from the body. ἐϋκνήμιδες is as the edition prints it (with a diaeresis), ‘well-greaved’, and εὔκηλοι is ‘at ease’. αἰθέρι is the dative of αἰθήρ, the bright upper air. πέπτατο is a pluperfect passive of πετάννυμι ‘spread out’, and ὀξεῖα ‘sharp’ describes the sun’s ray. νέφος … πάσης γαίης οὐδ’ ὀρέων is ‘a cloud over the whole earth or the mountains’, with genitives of place.

sentences.t:
μεταπαυόμενοι δὲ μάχοντο
ἀλλήλων ἀλεείνοντες βέλεα στονόεντα
πολλὸν ἀφεσταότες.
sentences.l:
and with pauses in between they fought,
shunning one another’s missiles full of groaning,
standing far apart.
sentences.i: pausing at intervals they fought, shunning one another’s missiles that brought groaning, standing far apart.
sentences.n: μεταπαυόμενοι is the present middle participle of μεταπαύομαι ‘stop in between’, so the fighting here goes in spells. ἀλεείνοντες is ‘shunning’, with the genitive ἀλλήλων, and βέλεα στονόεντα is the table’s ‘missiles that brought groaning’. πολλόν is the adverb ‘far’, and ἀφεσταότες is the perfect participle of ἀφίστημι, ‘standing off’.

sentences.t:
τοὶ δ’ ἐν μέσῳ ἄλγε’ ἔπασχον
ἠέρι καὶ πολέμῳ, τείροντο δὲ νηλέϊ χαλκῷ
ὅσσοι ἄριστοι ἔσαν·
sentences.i: but those in the middle were suffering pains from the mist and the fighting, and all who were the best were worn down by the pitiless bronze;
sentences.n: τοὶ δ’ is the men round the body, set against the others of 370–375. ἐν μέσῳ is ‘in the middle’, and ἠέρι καὶ πολέμῳ are datives of cause, ‘from mist and war’. τείροντο is ‘were worn down’ and νηλέϊ ‘pitiless’, as in the table. ὅσσοι ἄριστοι ἔσαν is ‘as many as were best’, that is, all the champions; ἔσαν is ἦσαν.

sentences.t:
δύο δ’ οὔ πω φῶτε πεπύσθην
ἀνέρε κυδαλίμω Θρασυμήδης Ἀντίλοχός τε
Πατρόκλοιο θανόντος ἀμύμονος, ἀλλ’ ἔτ’ ἔφαντο
ζωὸν ἐνὶ πρώτῳ ὁμάδῳ Τρώεσσι μάχεσθαι.
sentences.l:
And two men, not yet, had learned,
glorious men, Thrasymedes and Antilochus,
of Patroclus dead, the blameless, but still they said
him alive in the first uproar to be fighting with the Trojans.
sentences.i: But two men, glorious Thrasymedes and Antilochus, had not yet learned that Patroclus was dead, the blameless one, and still they supposed that he was alive and fighting the Trojans in the foremost uproar.
sentences.n: δύο … φῶτε … ἀνέρε are duals, ‘two men’, with κυδαλίμω ‘glorious’ (also dual) and the names in apposition; πεπύσθην is a dual pluperfect of πέπυσμαι (πυνθάνομαι) ‘learn’, without augment, ‘had learned’. Πατρόκλοιο θανόντος ἀμύμονος is a genitive, ‘of Patroclus dead, the blameless’, saying what they had not learned. ἔφαντο is ‘they said’, here ‘they supposed’, and takes ζωόν ‘alive’ with μάχεσθαι; ὁμάδῳ is ‘uproar’ (the noise of a crowd; the table keeps ‘throng’ for ὅμιλος), and the first uproar is the front of the fighting.

sentences.t:
τὼ δ’ ἐπιοσσομένω θάνατον καὶ φύζαν ἑταίρων
νόσφιν ἐμαρνάσθην, ἐπεὶ ὣς ἐπετέλλετο Νέστωρ
ὀτρύνων πόλεμον δὲ μελαινάων ἀπὸ νηῶν.
sentences.l:
And the two, foreboding death and the panic of comrades,
apart were fighting, since so laid his charge Nestor,
urging them to the war from the black ships.
sentences.i: And the two, foreboding death and the panic of their comrades, were fighting apart, since this was how Nestor gave his charge as he urged them from the black ships into the war.
sentences.n: τὼ δ’ is the same two men. ἐπιοσσομένω is a dual participle of ἐπιόσσομαι, which can mean ‘look at’ and ‘forebode’, the table’s ‘foreboding’ for ὀσσόμενος; it takes θάνατον and φύζαν ‘death’ and ‘panic’. νόσφιν is ‘apart’, from the throng round the body, and ἐμαρνάσθην is a dual imperfect of μάρναμαι ‘fight’. ἐπετέλλετο is the middle of ἐπιτέλλομαι, and ὣς ἐπετέλλετο … ὀτρύνων is ‘so he gave his charge, urging’ (the table’s rendering of this middle form); πόλεμον δέ is ‘to the war’ (-δε of direction), and μελαινάων νηῶν is ‘of the black ships’, with epic -άων.
